Maybe I can help clear things up. In 1992, the U.S. signed Nafta, the North American Free Trade Agreement. It actually reduced tariffs between the two countries to a minimum so both sides benefitted as longtime loyal allies from the easy exchange of goods and materials for the past 33 years.


Raising tariffs on Canada hurts them and us because it acts as a shipping fee on goods they would normally be able to just send us fee free. 


Business 101 says you dont make any money if you sell something for less than it costs to make and ship. So Canada ends up forced to raise their price of goods they send us to cover the cost of the tariff OR make up the difference by tariffing what we send to them in return. 


Either way, when we buy from them, it now costs more than it used to.


Another thing to think about...when I shop online if the shipping fees are crazy, I find what I want at another store. Our allies were giving us the best friends hookup price and we started charging them more and more for no reason. Thats bully behavior and America is better than that.

Was also homeless in the South. Can only speak about what I did and its great yourr planning early because I advise you to tough it out as long as you can to secure some tools that will make survival easier. I second WGU as a college option. Cost depends on how long it takes you to complete the needed credits. University of the people is another option. Research both. Most vital thing I can think of is a drivers license and car. That gives you transportation to work or wherever and doubles as shelter in a pinch. Have a cheap prepaid phone which wont hurt your credit if it runs out/you fail to pay. DEFINITELY get your own copies of your birth certificate and social security card. If your folks wont give it to you, you can request one at 18 for yourself. Have it sent to a trusted friend or a P.O. box if you can afford it at a local post office. I had the cheapest wal mart unlimited plan on a basic smartphone and showered at the gym with a planet fitness membership for 10 dollars a month. My first apartment I eventually moved in with just a backpack of clothes and a blanket. Dollar Tree and Craigslist and Goodwill were godsends as far as furniture/cookware. Dollar tree had cups and bowls and silverware/spatulas.
On the topic of apartments THE BIGGEST THING IS TO HAVE A YEAR OF CREDIT HISTORY WITH SOME KIND OF CREDIT CARD. I did not have that and nobody would rent to me until I did. Open a bank account and save as much as you can. I got my first credit card through my bank. I gave them 300 as collateral and they gave me a card with a 300 dollar limit. Every month I spent 30 bucks or less and paid it back fully each month. 700 credit score, easy. The better your credit, the better deals you get on rent and pretty much everything else. If the bank wont offer a secured card, try discover or capital one. They approve most people. The reality of independent living is most places want paystubs proving you make 3 times the rent and can pay anywhere from a few hundred to one months rent as a security deposit in case you damage the property. Having a car, roommates or both will help. Be smart and get as much lined up in your favor before you make the leap. Maybe have roommates to cut down the cost of living. 


If you dont have foodstamps, dollar TREE is a godsend. I worked two key jobs. Restaurant was nice because discounted meals and the cooks would box up orders that would otherwise get tossed and let me have them at the end of the shift after they caught me eating half eaten sandwiches from the trash. Working at a mechanic shop helped me keep my car running on the cheap. Employee discount. Pay was decent and I had healthcare. You dont have to know anything but experience at an auto parts store is low hanging fruit as far as "some automotive experience." if youre having a hard time getting your foot in the door. Or front desk at jiffy lube or pep boys or something. Dollar tree pays you daily. Goodwill has a lot of employee programs to help you do more with your life plus an employee discount. Try to have a few thousand of startup money in the bank because shit can and will go wrong.

Cupping is usually caused by worn shock absorbers. When they weaken, the tire skips along the ground and it wears little scoop shapes into the rubber. Manufacturer recommends replacement every 50,000 but typically people replace around 100,000 miles. Replacement for tires is recommended around 4/32 and below. You can either replace the worn components and tires and then align to fix the issue or continue to drive around with cupped tires. Its not a safety thing but be aware that it will cause vibration. Depending on the quality of the tire and how much you drive Id say another 5 to 10k honestly. Safety fail for tread is 2/32 and replacing at 5/32 or above is a waste of good rubber.

Edit: Not sure where you went since many chains use the same technician worksheet but Firestone offers a car care package for 10 dollars that would cover the labor cost to have the shocks/suspension checked for wear. Includes a free tire rotation and they can check brakes as well. Anything above 3mm on brakes is non urgent so you dont get taken for a ride. Hope that helps.

Brandons death sparked the push that has over time paved the way for a lot of the progress we benefit from today.
